value.overview: The Yellow-breasted Chat is a large, secretive songbird of dense shrublands and early-successional vegetation. It has olive-green upperparts, a bright yellow throat and breast, a gray face, white spectacles, and a white mustache-like stripe. Despite its warbler-like appearance, it belongs to its own family, Icteriidae. Males are noted for loud, varied songs that combine whistles, clucks, rattles, mews, and other unusual sounds.
value.classification: The Yellow-breasted Chat is Icteria virens, the only living species in the family Icteriidae. It was formerly grouped with New World warblers because of its appearance and behavior.
value.identification: This bulky songbird is about 18 centimeters long, with a relatively large head, heavy bill, long tail, and rounded wings. Adults are olive-green above and gray on the face, with a yellow throat and breast that contrast with the white lower belly. A white eye-ring extending toward the bill forms spectacles, and a white malar stripe borders the cheek. It usually stays hidden in thick brush, although males may sing from exposed perches during the breeding season.
value.rangeHabitat: The species breeds across much of the United States, southern Canada, and northern Mexico. It winters mainly from Mexico through Central America to western Panama. In Costa Rica it is a nonbreeding visitor rather than a resident or breeding species, occurring in suitable low, dense vegetation such as scrub, brushy clearings, pastures with scattered trees, forest edges, riparian thickets, mangroves, and disturbed woodland. It may be encountered during migration and the boreal winter, but is generally local and uncommon.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Birds breeding in North America move south in autumn, with many wintering in Mexico and Central America. Costa Rica is part of the species' wintering and passage range; it is not known as a regular breeding area there. Some individuals cross the Gulf of Mexico, while others migrate over land, often traveling at night.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place in dense, low vegetation across North America. The female usually builds a bulky cup nest one to eight feet above the ground in shrubs, vines, brambles, or tangled vegetation. Clutches typically contain three to six eggs, and incubation lasts about 10 to 12 days. The young leave the nest after roughly seven to 10 days. Most pairs raise one or two broods, and both parents feed the nestlings.
value.dietFeeding: Yellow-breasted Chats eat mainly insects and other invertebrates, including beetles, bugs, ants, bees, moths, caterpillars, grasshoppers, spiders, and other small prey. They glean food from leaves and branches in dense vegetation and may hold prey with their feet while feeding. Fruits and berries become more important outside the breeding season, including on wintering grounds such as Costa Rica.
value.behavior: The species is usually skulking and difficult to see, moving through shrubs with short flights and frequent pauses. Males sing loudly and produce an unusually varied series of whistles, rattles, chuckles, squawks, and other notes. During courtship or territorial defense, males may perform display flights with exaggerated wingbeats. Outside the breeding season, individuals are generally solitary and may defend feeding territories. Migrants often remain in low, dense cover during daylight.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population has declined in North America, with long-term monitoring indicating a substantial decrease since the 1960s. Trends vary regionally, and some western populations have been stable or increasing while many eastern populations have declined.
conservation.threats: The principal concern is loss of dense shrubland and other early-successional habitat as fields, clearings, and utility corridors become overgrown or are converted. Loss or degradation of riparian and wintering habitat may also affect the species. Migrating birds can be killed by collisions with tall buildings and communication towers, especially around strong nighttime lighting.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore native shrublands, brushy field edges, streamside thickets, and other early-successional habitats in both breeding and wintering areas. Manage some landscapes to maintain a changing mix of young forest and dense shrubs rather than allowing all open habitat to become closed-canopy forest. Reduce unnecessary outdoor lighting during migration and make windows safer for birds.
